utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. The Chamber hopes that you had a good time off. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina, et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. And, I think I would have to ask, first, after not having been in court for over four weeks, whether there are any procedural issues of an urgent character which needs to be addressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'll leave it to the Chamber when you wish to address the issue of the next witness, and how you wish to procedure, whether you wish to do that now or at some time later, but we do need to address that, I believe, somewhat urgently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think we should do it today. Mr. Hedaraly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HEDARALY
utterances.text: There are also a few issues regarding the experts that will be testifying, and once again we leave it to the Chamber, if that can be done at a later stage, but that also should be dealt with fairly soon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think, as a matter of fact that the next witness, that we should deal with that today, and as far as the expert witnesses are concerned, I prefer to deal with that not today. The Judges will further consider a few matters this afternoon so that we are fully prepared for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When I said today for the next witness, I'd like to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Misetic, are ready to call your next witness? I do understand that no application for protective measures exists and that the next witness would be Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, before you give evidence, the Rules of Procedure and Evidence require that you make a solemn declaration, the text of which is now handed out to you by Madam Usher. May I invite to you make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bajic. Please be seated. Mr. Bajic, you will first be examined by Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic is counsel for Mr. Gotovina. Mr. Misetic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajic. Would you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Mladen Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have the screen, please, 65 ter 1D2692. And with the assistance of Madam Usher, if I could give the witness a hard copy of his statement in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, on the screen, we have a witness statement that you gave to the Gotovina Defence on 21st of May, 2009. Do you recall giving this statement to an attorney for the Gotovina Defence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And is this -- is the statement that's on the screen the statement that you signed on the 21st of May, 2009?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, and that's the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Have you had a chance to review this statement before coming to court today?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And are there any changes that you believe need to be made to the statement, corrections?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No. It was compiled and accurately reflects what I stated at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you gave this statement, did you give it to the best of your knowledge and in accordance with the truth?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I told what I remembered, and everything I said was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I ask you the same questions today that you were asked at the time that you gave this witness statement, would you provide the same answers in court today that you did at the time that you provided those answers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, pursuant to Rule 92 ter I move to admit into evidence 65 ter 1D2692.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D1626.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As an administrative matter, I apologise, I failed to communicate this with the Prosecution before court today, but at paragraph 7 the witness discusses the basic criminal law of the Republic of Croatia. That's paragraph 7 of the statement which is 65 ter 629. And I would just simply move to admit that into evidence on the basis of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1627.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1627 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I have advised the witness of the procedure of reading a summary of the evidence, and with your permission I'd like to read out a summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness AG-5, Mladen Bajic, has been the Chief State Prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia since 2002. From 3 February 1992 to 6 December 1996 he was the Deputy Military Prosecutor at the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split, including during the period before, during, and after Operation Storm. In his statement, Mr. Bajic explains the laws that applied to the work of the military courts and the military prosecutor's offices during the time-period relevant to the indictment. The Military Prosecutor's Office operated within the system of the State Attorney's Office of the Republic of Croatia, with all the rules of subordination that existed there. The military prosecutor was subordinated to the State Prosecutor's Office and not the military. In terms of the relationship between the civilian and military police, Mr. Bajic testifies that the Ministry of Interior had general jurisdiction for conducting criminal processing and in cases where, in the course of the processing, it was established that the offence was under the jurisdiction of the military justice system, criminal processing would be taken over or conducted from the beginning by the military police. Mr. Bajic states that the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split consisted of the military prosecutor and a total of five deputy Prosecutors. Mr. Bajic testifies that after Operation Storm, there were a large number of criminal charges or reports registered. And that concludes the summary, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. One second, please. To start after the recess always causes some problems. It comes to my mind only that at 7.00 this morning, not only an issue of admission into evidence of a certain document was raised, but also - and I had not paid proper attention to that that - that the Prosecution had asked to deal with the matter before the commencement of the testimony of the witness. Ms. Gustafson, this is all early morning issues. Usually objections against whatever document to be admitted into evidence are dealt with if it comes to tendering it. Nevertheless, you have specifically asked to deal with the matter before the commencement of the witness -- of the testimony of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Misetic has informed us this morning that he no longer intends to tender the document, so the objection is withdrawn. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Which means that we can continue. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, in your statement you discuss the issue of the general jurisdiction of the civilian police. Let me ask you, if a soldier in the HV committed a crime in the period after Operation Storm but was demobilised prior to being indicted, who would have jurisdiction in that circumstance?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Exclusively the civilian police and the civilian judiciary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If could I have 65 ter 1D604 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, I'm going to show you a document prepared by you. It's dated 23 October 1995. I just want you to explain here -- if can you review the document and explain to us why you are forwarding here the criminal complaint to the civilian prosecutor's office, in this case.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Precisely for the reasons I mentioned a moment ago. The document shows that the person reported was no longer a member of the Croatian army, and therefore he fell no longer under the jurisdiction of the Military Prosecutor's office, but the civilian prosecutor's office in Split at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 1D604 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit D1628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1628 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Court in an example like this, let's look at the period after Operation Storm, how frequently did it occur that a person would be suspected of being HV because they were wearing a military uniform and after further investigation you established that the person was in fact not a member of the HV?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Such situations occurred quite frequently. In the aftermath of Operation Storm, according to the information I had at the time, a large number of members of the Croatian army were demobilised. Of course, all of them kept their uniforms. In the course of the proceedings, acting upon such criminal reports, we always verified what the status of the individuals was at the time the criminal reports were being processed because the military jurisdiction was solely tied to the membership of the Croatian army. Precisely for that reason, while acting upon a certain criminal report, we established that the person reported was no longer a member of the Croatian army. We had the obligation to forward the case to the regular military prosecutor's office, depending on the place where the crime was committed and depending on the territorial jurisdiction. We also had information to the effect that a large number of perpetrators dressed -- were dressed in uniforms or wore Croatian army uniforms solely for the purposes of facilitating the arrival at the crime scene and the perpetration of the crime itself. That's to say, to cover up their traces during the perpetration of the crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bajic, let me just check your answer here at page 12 lines 22 to 23, the answer as translated into English is that while acting upon a certain criminal report we established that the person reported was no longer a member of the Croatian army. Who did you have the obligation to forward the case to then?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: To the regular state prosecutor's office, depending on the subject matter and territorial jurisdiction. If the crime fell within the municipal jurisdiction, then it would be forwarded to the Municipal State Prosecutor's Office, or inversely, depending upon the level of the territory. We know that the -- this particular prosecutor's office in Split coved an area that was much larger than what other prosecutor's offices normally had.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your experience in the Military Prosecutor's Office, was it practice for the Military Prosecutor's Office to conduct a criminal proceedings and for commanders then to conduct parallel disciplinary proceedings for that criminal offence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Criminal procedures are quite distinct from disciplinary are procedures. Military prosecutor's offices and military courts had nothing to do with disciplinary procedures because there were separate military disciplinary courts and military disciplinary prosecutor's offices set up for disciplinary purposes. The decision as to whether minor or major disciplinary infractions, especially in the army, would be processed depended on the commander who received notice of a member of the army committing a breach of discipline. If the act was a crime, criminal proceedings would primarily be conducted because normally criminal proceedings also contained disciplinary proceedings for the particular infraction that the soldier was reported for. In the event that the soldiers are in fact convicted, they -- or detained, they automatically would be discharged from the Croatian army. Of course, this would not be the case in the event that the acts were minor violations of disciplines but only in the cases of major violations of discipline where criminal responsibility was also determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If you could just clarify a little bit your answer at page 14, lines 3 to 6 is: "If the act was a crime, criminal proceedings would primarily be conducted because normally criminal proceedings also contained disciplinary proceedings for the particular infraction that the soldier was reported for." I'm not sure that that is clear, and if you could just explain what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Can you point me to the item under which this is in the document? Because I have -- oh, you mean the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, you just answered my last question with that portion which was that you said that: "In the event it was a crime, criminal proceedings would primarily be conducted because normally criminal proceedings also contained disciplinary proceedings for the particular infraction." Can you explain a little bit what that -- what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I said that a disciplinary breach is -- a far less serious act. If the soldier committed a crime and this was reported to the military police by the commander, then the military police would report this to us, whereupon we would examine the act to see whether it satisfies elements of a crime. If so, criminal proceedings would be initiated. In that event, it would become moot to conduct disciplinary proceedings against a person because the persons unlawful conduct would primarily be reflected in the crime. This would roughly amount to the relationship between a crime and a -- and a misdemeanour, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In your experience in the Military Prosecutor's Office could a commander conduct his own investigation into a crime parallel to the investigation being conducted by the military police and the Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No. He was not able to. The commanders, just as was the case with all the state structures in the Republic of Croatia, they were duty-bound to file the report or inform the relevant organ - in this case, it was the military police - on all the information they had at the time, whereupon, the military police would launch and investigation in the pre-charge proceedings, file a report to the relevant Military Prosecutor's Office, which then directs the investigation depending on whether the facts are established or not, the Military Prosecutor's Office decides whether to file an official request for an investigation before a court, whether it will file an indictment, or whether in fact it will make a decision to dismiss the whole proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now let me ask you along these lines. A commander in the Croatian army, if he has information that a crime has been committed, what was the practice as to who he should inform of that criminal act?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I'm not a professional soldier and I cannot tell you what exactly the procedure was within a given unit, depending on the position the commander had within the hierarchy of the Croatian army. At any rate, once the commander learns of a crime having been committed or of suspicions that a crime was committed, the commander or the subordinates depending on what his practice was, would give notice of that to the military police who would then act on the information received. Depending on the seriousness of the crime, the military police would inform thereof the military investigating judge and the military prosecutor who jointly worked on the case. If the acts committed were not so grave, then the military police themselves would work on it. If the act involved was a serious crime and then the military police would first inform the military investigating judge who would notify in his turn the military prosecutor, and they would jointly work on what would then possibly become a future case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If a commander has knowledge that the military police already knows about a particular crime, does the commander, under the Croatian system applicable at the time, have an additional duty to report it again to the military police, if he is already satisfied that the military police knows about it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: It is difficult to answer hypothetical questions. Of course, if he knows that the military police is already seised of the event, it would be pointless to report to them the same thing. However, the commander is duty-bound to help, together with his officers, to secure evidence and facts that might be helpful for the future proceedings. At any rate, my answer to the question, whether he should report this once more is no, he should not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The question arises as to whether a commander could have reported a crime to the Military Prosecutor's Office directly. Can you explain whether he could have done that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, he could have done that. Not just the commander, but anyone, under the legislation at the time and under today's legislation, all the state bodies are duty-bound to file a report to the civilian police or the military police, as well as the competent prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If a commander knows that the military police has been informed about a crime, what further obligations does he have under the Croatian system applicable at that time?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: There are no obligations in terms of reporting except pursuant to requests of the military police or the public prosecutor or military prosecution to give certain information, data, which would enable the military prosecutors to determine whether a criminal offence exists and as to the criminal responsibility or liability.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 14 of your statement, you discuss the role of the military police. First, can you tell us which section of the military police you worked with most closely in the period during and after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Military Prosecutors, including me as Deputy Military Prosecutor, at the time I exclusively dealt with and conducted the Criminal Investigation Department within the military police, 72nd to 73rd Battalion of military police head quartered at Split, covering the same area that fell within the jurisdiction of the Military Prosecutor's office in Split and even broader area than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Court how -- or the system of cooperation between the military crime investigation police and the Military Prosecutor's Office? What were they obligated to do with respect to your office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The cooperation and communication could be divided into two parts, or groups of matters. General part pertains to the establishment of a general system of effective conduct and cooperation of military police and military prosecution service. This is conducted at working meetings where Military Prosecutors and deputies would attend on the one hand, and heads of the military police and crime investigation department within the military police on the other hand to work out effective and swift cooperation and exchange information about the work of the military police to make it as effective as possible. We have to bear in mind the fact is when the military police was established in 1992, it was peopled by personnel who had not had extensive experience in working in criminal cases and they had to be assisted by all those who were knowledgeable of those things within the system or by people who came into the service from public prosecutor's offices who now the ropes, so to speak. The other part of our joint work was work on specific cases, case work. For instance, after military police would file criminal reports to the military, or when anybody else would report something to the Military Prosecutor's Office by the regular police, NGOs, citizens or whoever, military prosecutor, pursuant to Article 41, I think that it was that Article defining the role of the public prosecutor, was duty-bound in the pre-criminal proceedings to direct the inquiries and to seek from the military police and instruct them what to do, to create the conditions -- to make a decision on such a criminal report, which means obtain information, facts, evidence, documents, whatever, which would enable the military prosecutor or the deputy military prosecutor seised of the case to determine whether the matter is a criminal offence or that there was no sufficient grounds for suggestion suspicion or that there was no criminal offence at all. Such cooperation was done in several ways. First, in writing, by sending memos to the military police from the Military Prosecutor Office, instructing them what to do pursuant to which Article of the criminal procedure act. In more complex cases we would have working meetings, military policemen there. Criminal investigation officers would come to the military prosecutor's offices and together with the deputy military prosecutor seised of the case, would tell them and agree on what should be done in the case. And thirdly, there were general meetings which were concerned with general matters of how to proceed, the effectiveness of work, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. You described the scenario where what happens once a criminal report comes into the Office of the Military Prosecutor. What about in a situation, for example, that the Military Prosecutor's Office hears something in the media, an allegation that the Croatian Army engaged in a criminal act in some location. Does the Military Prosecutor's Office, based on that information alone, have the authority to either open an investigation or request additional information or investigation by the military police?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Of course, public prosecutor's office, pursuant to the criminal procedure act of the time and today, is duty-bound to whenever they learn about a criminal offence, they have to make a note about that or prepare a note of information from the media, if it's reliable or indicative of a possible criminal offence. After that, the prosecutor has to seek from the military police or the civilian police, depending on the type, to make inquiries or prepare criminal investigation, if necessary, to see whether a criminal offence has been committed, and, if so, who was the perpetrator, and we had such cases in our practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Just to clarify your answer. Does that apply to both the public prosecutor's offices and the military prosecutor's offices in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, public prosecutors and military prosecutors had the same powers, but the difference was in the jurisdiction. If military prosecutors learned that a specific criminal offence had been committed on the basis of such information from the media or learned otherwise, they could prepare an Official Note and seek from the military police to do further inquiries, and we've had such cases, as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. The Court has seen examples of daily reports of the duty service of the crime police of the 72nd Military Police Battalion, and they are in evidence, and amongst other entities who were served with that would be the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split. Can you tell us why you would have been receiving such daily reports from the duty service?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: We received them for the deputy military prosecutor and the [indiscernible] -- prosecutor's office in general would be cognizant of what was going on on the ground and what were -- what was -- the military knew about possible criminal offences. Those reports do not report only on criminal offences. As you've seen, they contain information about other events or incidents that were not criminal offences. Military prosecutor or his deputy would read those daily reports, and there was enough ground for doing so. They would seek further information or file criminal reports on criminal offences where there was sufficient suspicion of such offences having been committed. In cases whose severity demanded that, after sometime we would check whether criminal reports have been filed, whether the case file has been opened, because criminal case files were not, as a rule, based on such daily reports but on such additional information. Those daily reports were just an announcement that certain reports may be forthcoming. It was a summary of further communications or filings that would materialise a couple of days down the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What were the duties of the military prosecutor in circumstances --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the counsel please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What were the duties of the a military Prosecutor in circumstances where the military prosecutor had information that a crime had been committed but the perpetrator of the offence was unknown?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: After receiving a criminal report by the military police or others against perpetrators unknown, the military prosecutor or the deputy working on the case would seek further inquiries from the military police, if they had filed such reports about persons unknown, instructing the military police to get witness statements, information, evidence, that may help identify the perpetrator, file charges, and process the whole case. Of course, in the military prosecution system, we had fewer criminal reports against perpetrators unknown, because if the perpetrators were unknown, then such cases would be sent to the civilian or regular public prosecutor's office because they had general jurisdiction. But there were situations, however, where injured parties or those filing reports, in their reports against persons unknown, would mention that the perpetrator was an unknown member of the Croatian Army, and then the military prosecutor would then, first of all, try to identify the perpetrator, given the presumption was that the perpetrator was an HV member, seek the military police to get involved, and after a while, if unsuccessful, forward the case to the general prosecutor system, since the perpetrator has remained unknown up to that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: In the KTN registers of the Split Military Prosecutor's Office, there are some entries for unknown perpetrators, and you've explained one of the circumstances. Would there by any other reason that there would be unknown perpetrators identified in the KTN registers of the Split Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Apart from the reason that I explained, when in a criminal report it was mentioned that a possible perpetrator -- or the unknown perpetrator, I correct myself, was a member of the HV, pursuant to the decrees that military courts and military prosecutors and military police worked, there were certain criminal offences where the military prosecutor had exclusive jurisdiction, crimes against Croatian Army, its materiel and munitions, they were registered -- such criminal offences were registered in the military KTN of the military not the civilian KTN registers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if we could have Exhibit D868 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, this is a report of items seized by the military police at a check-point on the 8th of August, 1995. Can you tell us what the procedure is or would have been or should have been if a military policeman seizes items at a check-point from a soldier who had improperly obtained possession of these items. What are the next steps?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Pursuant to those reports, and I can see that there were a number of them, military police had to conduct criminal investigation and with respect to each soldier that was controlled at the check-point, and they had to file criminal charges for theft or grand theft to the military prosecution office, confiscate such items and issue a receipt, because, ultimately, the court would hand down its decision on permanent or -- confiscation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you about a situation now where some fires have broken out in an area where it's it reported that members of the Croatian Army, some members, unnamed, were in the vicinity of the houses that are on fire. Who has jurisdiction to begin an investigation into that incident?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: You see, it is dubious on the basis of what you asked me, whether there are sufficient grounds to suspect that those members of the HV perpetrated that criminal offence or the perpetrators were completely unknown and possibly civilians. But regardless of that, in such a situation, forces of law as the law states have to undertake all the possible and necessary measures to secure evidence and to conduct inquiries or pre-criminal investigation. And in such a case, both the civilian police and the military police, whichever is closer to the scene, should do, something or if the perpetrators are unknown, then bodies of general jurisdiction would have primacy, which means civilian police, and if there's grounds to suspect that the perpetrators are military personnel, then the military police would be duty-bound to act.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have on the screen 65 ter 1D602, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: What we see on the screen, Mr. Bajic, is the monthly reports of the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split beginning in the month of July 1995. For example, if we go to page 4 of the document, it's signed by Ivan Simic. Can you tell the Court who that was?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Ivan Simic was the military prosecutor in Split. And previously Municipal State Attorney at Split, and Deputy Military Prosecutor of Split. He is a professional who, in 1992, was appointed as Military Prosecutor. But this is my signature on behalf of Ivan Simic and this is not Ivan Simic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, could you tell the Court then, did you prepare -- did your office prepare monthly reports in 1995, and, if so, why? And to whom were you sending them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Public prosecutor's offices, both municipal and county, are duty-bound to send a monthly operative report with statistics of their work and some major cases from their workload. They send such reports to their superior prosecution offices. The military prosecution officer had to do so to the prosecutor general's office of the Republic of Croatia on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I will tender 65 ter 1D602, which are the monthly reports from July to December of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, would you like to have them admitted as one batch or -- one batch.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1629.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1629 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, could you tell us were there circumstances after Operation Storm where, in fact, persons were -- who were HV were demobilised and then prosecuted through the civilian criminal justice system and if so, how frequent an occurrence was it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: After Operation Storm, this happened quite frequently, because a large number of HV soldiers were demobilised, and criminal reports filed while they were members of the HV, or it was presumed that they were, was forwarded to regular prosecution offices, to Split, Sibenik, Dubrovnik, et cetera, after verification that they no longer were members of the HV because membership of the HV was the condition for military prosecution. For military prosecutors to act on criminal reports up to the moment an indictment was prepared, because beyond that point, it was irrelevant which court took over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Would you -- would you expect that the statistics of the civilian court system, for crimes prosecuted after Operation Storm, would also include such categories of persons? In other words, they were HV at the time of the commission but demobilised prior to the filing of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, they were part of the statistics and records of regular prosecutors. And in terms of what I remember of the reports that we submitted, we had statistics of persons prosecuted or processed by both civilian and military prosecutor offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if I could have on the screen, please, 65 ter 308.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is a report that was sent by the Republic of Croatia to the Security Council, I believe, in January or February 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could go to page 12 in the B/C/S, please, and page 18 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: A part of the report includes statistics of crimes prosecuted after Operation Storm. And it reports on the military court in Split towards --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The next page in the Croatian, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It states that as of the filing of this report: "Proceedings are under way against 66 persons as follows. 63 persons are charged with the criminal offence of aggravated larceny, and three persons charged with the criminal offence of murder."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we go back two pages in English, looking at the bottom of this chart. The chart indicates that all 66 perpetrators in the military court in Split were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is that consistent with your recollections of how many crimes were processed after Operation Storm, for the crimes of larceny and murder, by the Military Prosecutor's Office, roughly speaking?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Well, I can only believe the data in front of me. But as per my assessment, this was really so. I do not doubt that we provided incorrect [as interpreted] information when sought to provide information and statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I tender 65 ter 308 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit D1630.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, at paragraph 17 of your statement, you indicate that there were a total of six persons in the Military Prosecutor's Office. I should say six prosecutors in the Military Prosecutor's Office, that one of them was -- was charged with covering the Zadar area and one of them was charged with covering Sibenik. Can you give us an assessment -- did you feel at the time and do you feel now that you had sufficient persons and resources to do everything that needed to be done in that area after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Well, Military Prosecutor's offices were established pursuant to a decree on the organisation of military judiciary dated 1992. That decree determined the number of officials, prosecutors and everything else. Apart from -- you said there were six people, we had a deputy military prosecutor in Dubrovnik. At the time military prosecutors and military judges, of course, were -- had a very large case load in terms of the number of cases, exceeding by several times the norm of -- the norm of cases for -- for each official, and for that reason, we worked almost 24/7, because the number of cases per military prosecutor was five times higher than that of ordinary civilian prosecutors. We had the military prosecutor and two deputies in Split; we had one deputy in Sibenik, and in Zadar and Dubrovnik respectively. Our colleagues in Split, including military prosecutor, would, on occasion, travel to Dubrovnik, Zadar, and Sibenik to attend trials to help our colleagues in criminal investigation in drafting of the indictments, and to help them by taking up some of their workload so that they could focus on their own cases, to help them tide over such dire times. And in connection with the work of Military Prosecutors, may I say that the enactment of that decree meant the following: The erstwhile deputy county or municipal prosecutors were transferred to military prosecutor offices which means that, in practice, I just pasted a label Deputy Military Prosecutor, instead of Deputy Public Prosecutor and wore a uniform, and everything else remained the same. In -- on the 6th of December 1996, the process was the opposite. I removed that label or sticker from my door and wore civilian clothes. Only some public prosecutors were transferred to the military prosecution services. We could use all the administrative and other resources which served the civilian prosecutor offices, they worked for us, in effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: You talk about having -- your work burden was five times that of the regular civilian prosecutor, and that you, after Operation Storm, were working 24/7. In addition to crimes committed by HV, how big of a burden did you have placed upon your office by the processing of crimes committed by persons who had participated in the so-called army of the RSK?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, we had a very high number of criminal reports filed against civilians and against individuals who were members of the enemy army. Such reports were primarily filed by the civilian police, and the cases had priority at the time, because the reports filed against members of the so-call SAO Krajina had to be processed first. Primarily, if it involved persons who were detained and such a practice continued until the Law on General Pardon was enacted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think we'll have an opportunities to look at the KTN registers later, but can you tell us why there are significantly more entries, for example, for armed rebellion, in the KTN registers of the Military Prosecutor's Office than there are, for example, for larceny, burning, et cetera, after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I don't understand your question fully. Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think it -- it should maybe be KT register.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: KT, sorry. I'm confusing KT with my Internet service. But I will fix that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The KT registers for the Split Military Prosecutor's Office, they have significantly more entries for crimes such as armed rebellion or terrorism than for, for example, for larceny, theft, murder, et cetera. Can you explain why there are substantially more entries for crimes that could be considered crimes against the state in the KT registers after Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That can be explained quite easily. In the aftermath of Operation Storm the Croatian army captured a great number of members of the enemy. At the same time, they came by information revealing the identities of the individuals who were members of units of the enemy army. I specifically remember receiving such information from the area of Vrlika which fell under the jurisdiction of the Split Military Prosecutor's Office. We came by lists of members of certain units of and, having verified identities through the MUP archives, as they were all -- or most of them Croatian citizens, we were able to file indictments against them for armed rebellion and other such crimes, as crimes against the -- the integrity of the territory, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bajic, let me quickly turn to a different topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could have on the screen Exhibit D680.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the law -- the amnesty law that was passed in September of 1996. Can you tell us, this amnesty law, does it cover crimes committed during Operation Storm that would not be classified as a war crime?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, it does. Under Article 1 of that same law, the definition is set out which states that the persons are -- amnestied who had anything to do with the armed conflict in the Republic of Croatia, and the amnesty is granted for the period between the 17th of August, 1995.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And the interpreter didn't hear the other date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And of course, the crimes involved were the ones comitted in relation to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the interpreter didn't hear -- it covers the period --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If can you start your answer again from where you said it covers the period of -- from when to when?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 17th of August 1990, and the 23rd of August, 1996, as stated in Article 1 of the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And you were -- before I cut you off, you said --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Of course, we have to bear in mind the fact that the act to which this law is applicable had to have something to do with aggression, armed rebellion, or armed conflict. Otherwise, it does not fall under this law. Furthermore, the amnesty does not apply to war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a good opportunity for a break, if the Court wishes to break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We'll have a break and we will resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic, you may proceed. I have French on my English channel at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, I'm going to turn now to your role as -- your current role as Chief State Prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have on the screen 65 ter 1D2940, please. And this is an exhibit that is currently not on our 65 ter exhibit list, Mr. President. We would seek leave to add it. It is a report from Mr. Bajic' office concerning the further clarification killings which, as the chamber knows, we were given additional time to try to investigate, and we would ask that we be granted leave to put this on the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections against adding to the 65 ter list.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. The only matter is that this was just disclosed to us on Friday, and in order to cross-examine we may need additional time but not a great deal, but over night at least. I don't know how long Mr. Misetic intends to go today. It may not be a problem anyway, but just to notify the Chamber of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the first step is adding it to the 65 ter list does not meet any objections. Therefore, leave is granted, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, do you recognise this list that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Actually, if we could get the --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is this the list that was provided to Gotovina Defence concerning the status of various killings that have been identified by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And I'm just going to draw your attention to one entry at the moment and I'll get back to it in a few minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: But if we could go to entry number 153.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This is the killing of Stevo Vecerina, and you can see some of the details there that were provided by your office and that the --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could perhaps use the Croatian version just so that the witness can read it across. Page 7 in the Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you can take a look at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And we'll flip it back to the English, Mr. President, so that the Court can take a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: This the status of that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And now if we could go to the English, which is page 6 in English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says your office states that today there was a request for investigation, investigatory actions, you are interviewing witnesses, and the investigation is ongoing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, I would ask that this exhibit be marked and I tender it into evidence, and I will be referring to it later again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I do understand no objections, but you would like to reserve your position as far as time to prepare for cross-examination is concerned. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours that will become Exhibit D1631.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D1631 is admitted into evidence. Ms. Gustafson, we will hear from you whenever you feel that you need more time. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, first as a general matter, in the time-period immediately after Operation Storm, and by that I mean August and September of 1995, can you tell us what information the Military Prosecutor's Office had that would indicate that Croatian Army personnel may be involved in the murder of Serb civilians during or after Operation Storm in the newly liberated areas, which were under your jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: The information we had came solely from the criminal reports filed before us at the time, and which had to do only with the area covered by Operation Storm. We also received information from the media on crimes committed in that region. However, the information we relied upon came solely from the criminal reports filed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, if could I have Exhibit D802 on the screen, please. And this is at -- if we can take a look at the cover page, and then we'll be going to page 4 in both the Croatian and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now, this is a report that was sent on the 11th of October, and it is by a Colonel Kozic sent to General Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could now go to page 4 in both versions, please. If we could scroll down to paragraph number 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: There's a report there that this is from the special operative action Varivode and it talks about -- there was a separate request from the MUP to include staff of the crime investigation military police of the military police administration to coordinate forensic processing of the unsolved murders of one or more of the civilians who remained resident in the newly liberated areas following military and police Operation Oluja ... And then the next paragraph says: "The engagement of the crime investigation military police to shed light on these serious criminal offences began on 2 October 1995, when the first working meeting was held at 0830 hours, attended by the administration of the RH MUP and the military police administration staff. It was at that meeting that this service received its first information of the murders, based on which it then acted. Namely, the crime investigation military police was informed of 11 cases in which one or more civilians were murdered by unknown perpetrators. Special emphasis was placed on cases which justified indications that the possible perpetrators or witnesses of a murder could have been members of the HV."

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And if we turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It says: "In only two cases information of a low level of verification concerning the participation of HV members was presented," then identifies the two cases as Gorsic and the second was in Zrmanja. "All other information pertaining to these or other murder cases pointing to possible involvement of HV members were of a much lower level of verification and did not warrant the involvement of military police crime investigators." Now, you were in the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split during this time-period and during OA Varivode. Is this information consistent with what your understanding was at the time of the possible involvement of HV members in murders of Serb civilians in the months of August and September 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: The document which has been shown to me and is on the screen is one that I am seeing now for the first time. As far as I can see, the military prosecutor mentioned here was not involved in these cases. I can also see that the entity responsible for all these cases was the civilian police which only sought the assistance from the military police in order to help them check the information that was of a low level of verification and which had to do with the possible involvement of Croatian army personnel. In -- therefore, the cases were conducted by the civilian police, and it was precisely the Gorsic and Varivode cases that were under the jurisdiction of the civilian police in Zadar first and then in Split. The information on the -- this type of crime came from the media, and there were no actions taken in respect of the military police as such, and, besides, these allegations later on turned out to be true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you -- I'm not sure if it was picked up. Can you explain again why you said no actions in this respect were taken by the military police as such?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: The document on the screen indicates that the structure responsible for the cases was the civilian police which called upon the military police to assist them in verifying information that was material for them for the evidence. So the main role was played by the civilian police; whereas, the military police was only charged with helping them out in identifying perpetrators. This is what follows from the document we have on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you just about your own recollection. Do you recall hearing information, whether from the military police or the media or any other source, that HV members were suspected of murdering Serb civilians during or after Operation Storm? And I'm asking you about the time-period August and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, I did hear, but I'm not sure if it was the Varivode-Grubori-Gosici cases, et cetera. I heard stories about murders and other crimes committed within generally speaking, but I can't tell you to which particular case the information was related. This is something that I don't know. Although initially the media reports did create an impression that the perpetrators were members of the Croatian Army. I can speak of the knowledge that I had, only through the cases that I was seised of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. If in fact the military police, at least as it is reflected in this document, came up with two cases as of the 11th of October, 1995 which had low level of verification concerning participation of HV members, if your office felt, based on media reports that there were other crimes that HV members may be involved in - crimes of murder, I should say - could your office have instigated its own proceeding without waiting for a report from the military police?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: This question is not specific, if I can put it that way. If a notice of general information was received of murders having been committed there, et cetera, one could not act upon such information. However, since we received information from our colleagues in Zadar and Sibenik, and I'm primarily referring to those prosecutors, had we received information from them, then we could have sought additional information from the civilian or military police pursuant to that specific information we received depending, again, on who the possible perpetrators were suspected of being.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split had, in fact, received such information from the civilian prosecutor's office, or the civilian police, or any other source, would that information be reflected in the KT register of the Split Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: It would not have been. That information would appear in a third register called KRDO which was the miscellaneous register for cases which did not yet have a criminal report, which did not such a degree of reliability as to indicate that a crime was committed. I have to go back to Article 41 of the Law on the Public Prosecutor's Offices which stated that the Public Prosecutor's Office was primarily the prosecution body and the police was the detection body. This is something that needs to be borne in mind when we're talking about inquiries into information that crimes had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now turning to the specific case of Varivode, can you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, let me preface this by saying that the witness may ask to move into private session, and I've advised him that he could ask if his answer would require revealing details of an ongoing investigation. And so he may ask the Chamber for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: My question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that Mr. Bajic has understood your guidance being a professional himself. Mr. Bajic, you heard what Mr. Misetic just said, and that's --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll hear from you if there's any need to go into private session. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, my question is: The Chamber has heard already from your deputy, Mr. Galovic, about the investigation and Prosecution of the Varivode case in the 1990s. The Chamber has also heard from Mr. Zganjer in the Varivode case. My question to you is it's now been 14 years almost since the Varivode Murders. Can you explain to the court why that crime remains unsolved and why it has taken so long for the State Prosecutor's Office and the police and other relevant institutions to cover -- either uncover the perpetrators or pursue charges against those who have already been suspected of the crime. And if your answer requires private session, please ask the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, can we move into private session, please, since what I'm about to say is partly bound by official secret status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, we should move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, if I could ask you more generally, if you could -- you've had an opportunity to look at the Prosecution's further clarification of killings, and can you give us some of the factors from your perspective that hindered the ability of the Croatian state authorities to investigate or prosecute some of the unsolved killings that have been identified by the Prosecution in its further clarification schedule.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe I should go back to what I stated earlier. To wit, after the homeland war, the situation was that crimes occurred in Croatia, whereby either witnesses or the suspects were in other countries. Cooperation between police and prosecution bodies in the region was relatively weak and only over the past couple of years, thanks to different initiatives, we today have such a level of cooperation which enables us to bring some investigations further ahead to -- closer to the perpetrators and criminal prosecution. I know about Croatia but also in other countries of the region, I know that by using information, exchanging of evidence and data, including the ICTY, we've managed to conclude successfully some criminal prosecutions of war crimes in the territory of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you, following up on your question about -- or your answer about witnesses or suspects being in other countries. Let's take the example, if the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY was able to interview a witness in Serbia in the late 1990s or in the early part of this decade, would the Office of the Prosecutor of the ICTY then share that information with your office, contact you to let you know that they have obtained evidence of a killing from a witness in Serbia and ask you to pursue the matter further?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: In principle, on the basis of international cooperation and the relations that we had in place, from the OTP of the ICTY, we received two cases one was it's Ademi-Norac case and the one more is the code-named Atlantis. And on the basis of material received from the ICTY's Prosecution office in the coded -- in the code-name Operation Atlantis, we opened an investigation in the area of Poziga [phoen]. We have a first instance court decision in that case, which involves dozens of victims. Others, no. Only at the end of 2005 when the memorandum of understanding were signed and also in connection with the exit strategy of the ICTY when we realized that the prosecution services in the region had to take over the task of prosecuting the perpetrators of crimes that had not been processed or detected, only then did things move ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's look at the example that I had highlighted earlier from Exhibit D1631, which is scheduled killing -- I'm sorry, further clarification, killing 153, which is Stevo Vecerina, and it's actually an event that relates to numbers 150 through 154 of the Prosecution's further clarification schedule. Mr. Bajic, the Chamber heard testimony about this incident from Ms. Marija Vecerina and that transcript testimony is at page 6704 through 6754. Now, Ms. Vecerina had provided some evidence to the Office of the Prosecutor in the early part of this decade; and there was another witness who also provided a statement in the late part of the 1990s to the OTP. Can you tell the Court when was the first time that the authorities of the Republic of Croatia received notice that these five individuals had been potentially murdered?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I personally do not know anything about this specific case of Vecerina, but I have to go back to the fact that in 2001 in Knin we disinterred some bodies and 300 bodies were found there on that occasion. The process of identifying those bodies is still ongoing, and, as far as the current results are concerned, 124 individuals have been identified, and for a majority of them it has been established that they were killed and the cause were fire-arms wounds to the chest, head, and abdomen. Most of them concerned information that we had received about the crimes occurring in the territory and concerning the cases that we mentioned today, Gorsic, Varivode, et cetera. I do not know anything about this particular case, but I must mention that after 2001, and after those individuals were identified, and when we heard explanations from experts saying that those persons were murdered at point-blank range, we opened a number of cases in the area of Zadar and Sibenik, and this is -- this goes a way of explaining why many of those cases have been registered as opened in 2004. Most of them are registered in the KRDO registers, meaning that there is no sufficient evidence pointing to a criminal offence or that we have no information about the perpetrators. Another thing, a number of relatives of those people that we had no information who had been killed there, in the mid-2000 -- started filing criminal reports or filing lawsuits about the killings after they'd returned to Croatia or after they'd learned that intensive work is going on in Croatia to uncover the perpetrators of such war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me ask you generally speaking then, if -- was it the case that in fact the authorities of the Republic of Croatia in many cases didn't have any information that -- from witnesses that someone had been killed until the filing of such criminal reports or lawsuits sometime in the middle part of this decade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: We have plenty of information and cases opened in such a matter -- manner. There's another fact which is noteworthy, and that is claims for damages filed by injured parties related to the pre-criminal investigation cases, and for those claims for damages to be valid, criminal prosecution against persons unknown have to be initiated, and this is another source of information that murders or crime -- criminal offences had been perpetrated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Now my question to you is: Is there a reason that you know of that information, for example, witness statements given to the Office of the Prosecutor about killings that may have been given to the office in the late 1990s or in the early part of this decade, why didn't you request that -- such information from them earlier than the middle part of this decade?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: For us to be able to seek information, we first had to have that information. In similar cases where we had information about criminal offences, we sought assistance from the OTP. For instance, in a specific case of Lora, in that case we sought information, and I believe that this was the first case where we petitioned the OTP to find in their archives information or evidence pertaining to that case and to deliver to us such information or evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have an understanding of why that information, once it came into the possession of the OTP, wasn't turned over until the middle part of this decade, turned over to your office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I do not know that, but I presume that that information was supposed to be used in the proceedings before this Tribunal or cases prosecuted by the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: And because of the fact that the Prosecutors in the region know, and it is generally known that in the ICTY's archives there is ample information and evidence about crimes committed, documents that can be used for local criminal prosecution and investigation in Bosnia, Croatia, Serbia, for that reason, we set up a joint system to facilitate the obtaining of documents that the countries of the region or prosecutors of the region could use in prosecuting war crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: The Chamber has also received evidence, and this is Exhibit P2345 and P2402, this is a report prepared by the Croatian Helsinki Committee about killings that took place -- allegedly took place during and after Operation Storm, can you explain to the court why more killings weren't processed on the basis of the Helsinki Committee report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything specifically about why things or more has not been done pursuant to the Helsinki Committee's report. I know that that report, as a body of information in possession of the Helsinki Committee, was forwarded to the competent police stations and departments, and that they must have done what they could have done on the basis of the information so provided. In respect to the public prosecution service, I can tell that you all the information which was corroborated by documents and evidence, they were processed and, over the past couple of years, this approach has been better and results have been better in terms of prosecuting such crimes than they had been previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the Croatian Helsinki Committee has ever turned over a witness statement or other evidence to either your office or the Croatian police with respect to any killing that's identified in the Helsinki Committee report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I must admit that I do not recall receiving such reports. But, at any rate, had they been received by the Prosecutor General, they would have been processed, forwarded to the competent police authorities for further processing, particularly if they had been corroborated by certain documents or evidence contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: When I say I do not recall, I distance myself intentionally because I don't know which report you specifically refer to so I don't want to make a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let's me go back to an answer that you gave at page 13 line 1 and ask if could you explain it a bit further. In that answer you said we also had information that a large number of perpetrators were dressed in uniforms or wore Croatian army uniforms solely for the purposes of facilitating the arrival at the crime scene and the perpetration of the crime itself. That's to say, to cover up their traces during the perpetration of the crime? Can you explain a little bit what you mean, how would they cover up the crime by being in a Croatian Army uniform, and how would it facilitate their arrival at the crime scene?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Well, on the basis of the document that you showed me on the existence of a check-point, it is evident that after it had been observed by the competent authorities, that property crime was going on in the area covered by Operation Storm, certain control mechanisms were put in place to prevent such occurrences. This is beyond question. Of course, civilians could not gain access undetected to the territory which was encompassed by the military police Operation Storm, and obviously it would be easier for them to pass check-points if they wore military uniforms. These are the facts that we noticed when we processed certain cases, specific cases, because after -- after some of them were apprehended, brought before court, or when criminal proceedings were initiated against them, it was established that they had been demobilised, that they had ceased to be members of the HV, but they continued to wear HV uniforms. Another thing, which was apparent to everybody living in Croatia at the time, was that people used to wear either whole uniforms or parts of uniforms, regardless of their status in the Croatian Army. They simply wore them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You were both obviously the Deputy Military Prosecutor in Split and at all times have been a prosecutor since that time, culminating in your current position of the Chief State Prosecutor of the Republic of Croatia. Can you give us your assessment as to how effectively the criminal justice system functioned in the liberated areas after Operation Storm, in your assessment?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: You see, I can only speak in hindsight and starting from the standards that we have today. I said initially that both the military police and the military justice system and the justice system in general had only been developing or evolving at the time. Many investigating judges, military and civilian prosecutors -- or, rather, their numbers were quite few in relation to the cases emerging. I will speak for the Military Prosecutor's Office, and that's why I said that we worked 24/7, all the three prosecutors who were working in Split had extensive experience from their previous career, and we had the support of the Civilian Prosecutor's Office whose resources we used, and we still had problems with insufficient personnel. For this reason, quite a few cases were not processed as well as they should have been, speaking in hindsight, and have not therefore created conditions for trials to be carried out effectively. The mistakes committed at the time still pose problems which we are confronted with in processing these same cases. The military police was set up only in 1992. The way in which the military police was organised had to be -- had in fact personnel that was quite inexperienced, and time had to pass in order for them to gain the requisite level of experience. Their skills, again, were coupled with the insufficient numbers of officers seised of cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat that last sentence again, please.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say was that the number of forensic officers or the criminal investigation officers of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions which the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split cooperated with was quite low, and their ability to act in certain cases was called into question. In other words, they were unable to respond to all the requests for forensic examinations that they received from competent military prosecutors; plus, these same individuals, in the early days of the war, were active participants in war activities as soldiers as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Is there any -- you indicated that some of the case weren't -- that there were mistakes and some of the cases weren't adequately processed. Can you -- in the addition to the factors that you have already stated, are there any other factors that would have caused or that you believe caused those cases to be inadequately processed, in addition to the lack of experience of military police?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: I don't know what it is you're referring to, and I can't answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask it a different way. Was there any -- from your experience at the time, was there an intention on the part of certain individuals in your experience to not prosecute crimes committed by Croats against Serbs or Serb property?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No. I personally was not, exposed to any sort of pressure from anyone. No such conversations were even broached with me, and as far as I know, my fellow colleagues from the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split did not have similar experience either. We, as military prosecutors or deputies, better said, communicated in our work solely with criminal investigation police officers, and that was the level at which we communicated with the Croatian army. Perhaps the military prosecutor himself had a higher degree of communication with them. As far as we were concerned, these were officers of the 72nd and 73rd Military Police Battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Based on your knowledge of the work of the Military Prosecutor's Office in Split, was your office uninhibited in its ability to prosecute Croats for crimes against Serbs, if you felt the evidence justified it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Misetic. Could I receive indications as far as times for cross-examination are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't have any questions for the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will have only a couple of questions. So it wouldn't take more than, let's say, 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I expect to be quite some time, probably the remainder of today and most of tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, are you ready to cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, Mr. Mikulicic is counsel for Mr. Markac, and he is next in line to examine you, or cross-examine you now. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Bajic. As we speak the same language, I kindly ask you to make a slight pause before answering my questions so that the interpreters could accurately reflect our conversation. Can you please clarify a constract [as interpreted] from the Croatian criminal legislation; namely, the filing of a criminal report against a perpetrator unknown. Initially, you said that, save in exceptional cases, such criminal reports were filed before the civilian police or civilian prosecutor's offices. Whose duty was it, therefore, to investigate into and identify the perpetrators of the crime contained -- or crimes contained in the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Before answering the question, I would like to recall the jurisdiction of the military court and Military Prosecutor's Offices.
