Their jurisdiction was over crimes committed against members of the Croatian Army and for the crimes committed against the Croatian Army; in other words, the military hardware, et cetera, that was the basic division of jurisdiction. If a criminal report -- or, rather, the criminal report is filed by law enforcement personnel which, by definition at the time, included the regular civilian police of the MUP, and the military police, each within their own respective remit, which included the matters that I referred to and had to do with the military police. If a crime is committed against the armed forces, or in relation to combat assets, in that case, regardless of the fact that a perpetrator is unknown, the criminal report is always addressed to the Military Prosecutor's Office. However, if a crime is related to -- or, rather, if the crime is of the ordinary crimes which are not qualified and where the perpetrator is unknown, the regular prosecutor's office, or, rather, the civilian police have jurisdiction. To the best of my recollection, the situation was such that there were indications of the fact that the perpetrators of crimes were members of the HV, either because they wore the HV uniform at the time, or because some of the members of the HV knew that the perpetrators were members of the HV. In such cases the criminal reports would be filed to the Military Prosecutor's Office. However such cases were few. The Military Prosecutor's Office would, together with the military police, have the priority task of establishing whether the perpetrators were indeed members of the Croatian Army and therefore military personnel. If they established that the individuals were not HV members or if they failed to come by additional information definitely pointing to the membership of the HV, they would forward the case to the regular civilian prosecutor's offices. A handful of cases which involved perpetrators unknown that we had came under the jurisdiction of the civilian police and the civilian justice system.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: An incident occurred in a given area resulting in deaths, an X/Y unit was active in that particular area. The civilian police was given notice of that incident, and according to what you told us the civilian police had the duty to initiate the pre-criminal proceedings with a view to identifying the perpetrators. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: In principle, yes. If it is -- there is a high degree of probability that the perpetrators were HV members. This was an issue on the ground where commanders of both the civilian police and the military police, or the officers who were involved in it, cooperated on. If this was something that they were able to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the subject matter jurisdiction of either the civilian or the military police, they were precisely the competent bodies, i.e., the police who were supposed to identify the perpetrators and investigate and collect evidence?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is the law enforcement agencies who are charged with crime detection and not the prosecutor's offices, either the military or the civilian ones. This is what Article 41 of the Law on Public Prosecutor Offices states, and the prosecutor's office would only direct and advise the civilian or military police, in order to allow them to gather enough evidence or facts to complete the criminal processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Based on your personal knowledge and experience, was it the duty of the commander of the unit to take certain steps at the same time with a view to identifying perpetrators who were, at that point, unknown to that same commander?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Once the commander of the unit has reported the event to the military police, he can -- he cannot conduct a parallel investigation. This is something I know of and this is something I told Mr. Misetic. The fact of the matter is that the commanders of units were, on their part, duty-bound to assist the military police in establishing all the relevant facts as expeditiously as possible which it needed in order to solve the case. Similarly, they were supposed to assist the military prosecutor whenever he sought direct assistance from the unit, in providing him with all the relevant information, which would enable him to make decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Based on your experience and recollection, what was cooperation like between commanders and Military Prosecutors, where Military Prosecutors sought information from them? Did commanders, for the most part, accommodate such requests from military prosecutors, or did they perhaps exert pressure for certain courses of action not to be taken?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Initially they were very forthcoming. There was some problems but we resolved them through their superior commanders, and we were able to be successful in these exercises. In principle, they were forthcoming and there was no pressure excerpted on military prosecutors in order not to prosecute some matters. I don't know which year this was, when we processed one of the commanders of the 73rd MP Battalion in fact. Therefore, if he wasn't able to secure such sort of status for himself, then I'm sure he wasn't able to do so for others either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Once you were appointed to the duty of the State Prosecutor General of the Republic of Croatia, did you ever receive from a municipal or county public prosecutors to the effect that they had been under pressure from someone not to prosecute Varivode, Gosici, Grubori and similar cases?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That concludes my examination, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Hedaraly, will it be you who will cross-examine the witness? And I wonder whether it would -- or, no, you're just assisting Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson, would you prefer to start now and have to interrupt after 10 to 15 minutes, or would you rather start after the next break? Then we first have a break, and we resume at 25 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, you will now be cross-examined by Ms. Gustafson. Ms. Gustafson is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Bajic.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If could I have 65 ter 7380 up in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, do you recall an interview you had with members of the Office of the Prosecution on the 13th of August, 2009?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is the document you see the screen the note that was prepared following that interview?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And did you have an opportunity at the time to review that note and make corrections to it?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And are the contents of that note accurate, and do they reflect the truth, as far as you are aware?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if I asked you today the same questions you were asked when you gave the interview on the 13th of August, 2009, would you give the same answers that are stated there in that note?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender 65 ter 7380, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And since I do not hear from the other Defence counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2603.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. It is practice which has slowly developed here that also during cross-examination 92 ter statements are admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have a few questions before I want to turn to the next document, but I'd just like to warn the Registrar that it's very large, and it's 65 ter 7370 in case that assists him in having it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bajic, you stated that in August and September 1995, you were working in the Split Military Prosecutor's Office and you were based in Split. During that time-period, did you ever travel to the former Sector South or to any of the other areas that were liberated during Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: If you mean by that Zadar and Sibenik, yes, my answer is in the positive. Sinj as well. Yes, I did travel. But I did not visit the area of Knin and the surrounding area there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So the closest you got to Knin, would that be the area of Sinj?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it right that, as the deputy -- as one of the deputy military prosecutors located in Split, you didn't actually handle case that arose out of the liberated areas. Your cases arose out of the Split areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Primarily so, yes. To tell the truth, I would occasionally attend trials in the cases of the military court when it sat in Dubrovnik, Sibenik, and Zadar.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Do you recall ever participating in any trial dealing with a case of burning or looting or killing that occurred in the liberated area in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Allow for such a possibility, but I cannot recall specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And is it right that the cases that arose out of the liberated areas were generally dealt with by the deputy military prosecutors based in Zadar and in Sibenik?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Well, deputies in Sibenik and Zadar changed. None of them performed their full term of duty; colleague Zganjer was in Sibenik, then after them, Ivic; in Zadar Ardena Bijlo [phoen] and, I think, Denono [phoen], were at different times deputy military prosecutors there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say that your main source of information on crimes being committed in the liberated areas after Operation Storm was from the criminal reports that were filed with the Split Military Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. As I stated, criminal reports, or reports that we used to receive from the military police were the sole source of communication and information about what was going on in that area, apart from the reports in the media, which were accessible to all, but they were less specific than what we received in criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That actually brings me to my next question about information you received from the media, which you were also asked about in direct examination. And in answer to one of those questions, you referred to the division between the prosecution section of the criminal justice system and the police, and stated that the police were the primary body responsible for crime detection. And my question is: In general, would the information contained in a media article contain sufficient information to form the basis of a criminal report or to launch an investigation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: You see, I can discuss this in two ways. One, is from my position of a deputy military prosecutor, and information that such a person would receive during their everyday activities, or while on duty, and whatever information received during my duty hours, I would register in appropriate registers. The other matter are information received by the military prosecutor and -- who would decide which deputy is going to be in charge of which matter. All information received by Military Prosecutor's Office, either during duty hours or in other hours, would be registered in the appropriate register governed by the Law on Prosecutor Services, the KT, KTR, KTN registers and all the others that I mentioned in being interviewed by you which is reflected in this Official Note. Another matter is when we talk about competence of civil police and prosecution service. Civilian police has general jurisdiction when -- in cases where it is not known who is the perpetrator or where there is no indication -- justifiable indication that the perpetrator may be a military -- member of the military organisation. And --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- Mr. Bajic. I just wanted to get back to my question, which was just whether information you may have seen in the media would have been sufficient, in your view as a prosecutor, to form the basis of a report or to launch an investigation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Of course, there are insufficient -- if there were such information there were individual information, and my colleagues who were seised of those separated them from the other information and acted upon them, but they were, as such, not sufficient, generally speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 7370, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, the document that should be coming up on your screen shortly is the KT register for 1995. And you have explained the three log-books in your statement. In the note of your interview to the Prosecution, you referred to the KT, KTN and KTR log-books, or registers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, KTR is in the translation explained as expansion unknown. Is there any way to --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If could you explain to His Honour, Mr. Bajic, what the KTR register contains.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: The KTR register is a register where information and data is going to be entered into where information did not have the character of a criminal report, because they do not contain sufficient elements to lead the prosecutor to a conclusion that it went for a criminal offence or a -- perpetrator of a criminal offence. The R means "miscellaneous," which means that all other matters are going to be entered into that register. In KT, we have entries on criminal offences where perpetrators are known and in the KTN we entered criminal offences where the perpetrators are unknown, so the R, meaning "miscellaneous," contains entries on all other information which could not be classified into the previous two registers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if subsequently information was obtained that indicated that an entry in the KTR register did constitute a crime, would that then be transferred to either the KT or the KTN register?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. It would be transferred into one or the other, by either detecting the perpetrator or identifying the perpetrator, or by -- while investigations of KTR entries being conducted, would unearth indications that would lead the prosecutor to conclude that a criminal offence has been committed, but the perpetrators is unknown, so that such an entry would be transferred into the KTN, the perpetrators unknown register under a different number. There's another detail is [as interpreted] important. Prosecutors could not approach the courts on of the basis of entries in the KTR, whenever court is petitioned to examine witnesses or undertake any other action to be done by the investigating judge, the prosecutor had to transfer entries from the KTR into either of the other two per the rule -- per the rules of the service. Of course, I'm not saying that this was done in each and every individual case.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And if you look on your screen --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could have the original brought up --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- do you recognise this page as a page from the KT register in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you have explained this register and the way the entries were recorded already, and that's in -- reflected in paragraphs 5 and 6 of the note of your interview with the Prosecution. So I'd just like to look at a few entries so that this is clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 38 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in this document only the column headings have been translated into English as well as certain abbreviations.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could look at entry 796, which is, I believe, the second entry on the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bajic, this entry would have the number KT 796; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this would be a report from the 72nd Military Police Battalion, 3rd Company, Zadar; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Correct. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the criminal report number is 291/95?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the sixth column, this is a report against a suspect named Frane, Mihanovic, and the victim reflected in the 8th column is unknown; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct. NN, meaning person unknown.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in the next column, that indicates the provision of the Criminal Code and the date of the commission of the crime which, in this case is a case of theft and aggravated theft; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, theft and aggravated theft. That's the qualification of this criminal offence. It could be said Articles 125 and 126 depict criminal offences of theft and aggravated theft, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 62. And just for the court and the parties' reference, the entry we just looked is also reflected in Exhibit P2553 which lists the criminal reports of the Zadar Military Police Company. If we could look at entries 884 through to 887 on this page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you've explained in your interview note with the -- interview with the Prosecution that military units sometimes referred criminal reports to the military prosecutor. And if you look at entry 884, it says: "MO-GS, ZZP Split. VP 1108 Drnis." Now, Military Post VP 1108 is the 142nd Home Guard Regiment. Does this entry indicate a criminal report received from that unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's exactly it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we look at entry 886 at the bottom of the page. This is a report from VP 2138, Netkovic, which is the 116th Home Guard Regiment. And this, I take it, would a report from that unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the crimes being reported here are Articles 153 and 154 of the basic Criminal Code. And those crimes are failure or refusal to obey an order, and refusing to receive and use arms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. That would it be, as far as I can tell from the reference number and the qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 100 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, I'm just trying to identify, you said VP 2138 Netkovic, and that was in relation to -- oh, that was 884, 886.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I believe it's not on the screen anymore. It's a little further up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm just trying to follow -- yes, yes, I see --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 885.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yep. One second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could move to page 110, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you mind to go back to the previous one, because I have some difficulties in --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That was page 62.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes, you read for 886, report from VP 2138 Netkovic. Let me just have a look. I see VP 110 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, that must be 885. Is that my confusion?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I may have misspoke.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, on page 67, line 6, you said, "And if you look at entry 886 ..." and then you started reading what apparently is in 885 instead of 886. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sure it is, Your Honour. I apologise for the confusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just trying to follow every step of question and answer. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go to page 110. And to the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Bajic, if you could look at entry 1056.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is a criminal report from PUZK, PP, Gracac. That would be the police station -- Gracac police station within the Zadar-Knin police administration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this entry would reflect receipt by the Split Military Prosecutor of a criminal report filed directly by the civilian police where the information indicates the perpetrator -- or the suspect is a HV member; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we could go to page 120, to entry 1089, which is -- right ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this entry says: "OP DO Knin," and then there is a KT number and a KU number. And this entry reflects a file being transferred from the Municipal Prosecutor's Office in Knin to the Split Military Prosecutor, where the information in the possession of the prosecutor indicates the suspect is a HV member; is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here the Municipal Prosecution Office of Knin refer the case to the Military Prosecutor's Office, from its KT register, accompanied by the appropriate KT register number, against three persons. Out of those three, two are mentioned as being members of the Croatian Army.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. So it's fair to say that every criminal report received by the Split Military Prosecutor's Office against a known suspect -- from whatever the source, would be recorded in this register; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this procedure of municipal or county prosecutor's offices transferring files to the military prosecutor, where they discover that the suspects, or one of the suspects is a HV member, was that a mandatory procedure? Where the civilian prosecutors required to transfer their files in such circumstances?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Because they did not have jurisdiction for further actions, if they established that the reported person is a Croatian soldier. And pursuant to all laws and regulations, the jurisdiction is in the hands of the Military Prosecutor's Office and the military courts.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you were asked in your direct examination about HV members being demobilised prior to the filing of an indictment. If the -- if the criminal report was filed when the individual was an HV member, then they were subsequently demobilised before the indictment was issued. The criminal report would still be reflected in this register; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: It could be found in the register, but the register would also have an entry stating that the case was deferred to one of the civilian regular prosecutor's offices. It would state the date of deferral or referral, and the entire entry would be crossed out with a line, meaning that the case no longer lay within our jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And in relation to the filing of criminal reports by military units, if a military commander or a military officer within the Split Military District became aware of a member of the -- of a Split Military District unit committing a crime and he reported that crime to a prosecuting authority, is there any other prosecuting authority, aside from the Split Military Prosecutor, that he would report that crime to?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No. If he filed a report before the Military Prosecutor's Office, he met his duty under the Law on Criminal Procedure; whereupon, the Military Prosecutor's Office would formulate a case and send requests for inquiries and criminal processing to the police, depending on the contents of the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Could I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2604.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2604 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would also like it tender the KT register for 1996. I have no questions on it. If Your Honours would like me to show it to the witness, I'm happy to. If I -- if I could just tender it from the bar table with the 65 ter number I could also do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If the parties agree on the documents have you in mind to be those registers, I think there would be no need to show it to the witness. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We have no objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Also not with the description of the document, that ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I trust Ms. Gustafson will call up the right 65 ter number, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I hope it is 65 ter 7371, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar, that would ...

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit P2605.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could 65 ter 7372 brought up on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, the document that should be coming up shortly is the KTN register for 1995. And while that's coming up, if I could just ask you the criminal reports received against unknown perpetrators were received, generally speaking, from the same sources as those for the KT register, and by that I'm referring to principally the military police, civilian police, civilian prosecutors?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Although the order was somewhat different. First, the military police, then the civilian police, and then the rest.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't quite understand that. The order was somewhat different from -- from what?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Military police above all, followed by the civilian police and the others. But, no matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Is that the portion of the KTN register you see on the screen for 1995?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I have the same question with this register as with the KT register. Is it correct that every criminal report received by the Split Military Prosecutor's Office, from whatever source, against an unknown perpetrator and every criminal file against an unknown perpetrator transferred from a civilian prosecutor would be recorded in this register?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, against an unknown perpetrator, yes. It was mandatory.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So together the KT and the KTN registers represent a comprehensive record of the criminal reports received and transferred criminal files to the Split Military Prosecutor's Office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: That's right. One most note that the KTR register also contains a number of potential reports that may have subsequently been referred to one of these two registers. It only depends on the time-line and the dates you're looking at. But, in principle, yes. All the reports were contained either in the KT or the KTN registers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, could I seek clarification. The KTN register, we have the original on our screen at this moment, and I have the English translation. Under 8 in the English translation we see "DO." Under 9, we see "MUP." Under 10 in the original it says "DO," where in the translation it says "MUP." And under 11, the original says "MUP" whereas the English translation says "DOD" which is a unexplained yet -- I have not looked at the other pages yet, but at least it seems that 10 and 11 are not fully consistent in their presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'll request a revision of the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and then perhaps also a further explanation for DOD which seems not to appear in the original. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could go to page 3 of this document and entry 69, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, you can see from the second column this is a report received on the 20th of October, 1995. And in the third column, the reporting authority, is that a report received from the Military District Split, duty service?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Split Military District, duty service and number.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the column for the nature of the crime and the date of the crime, this is Article 155 of the Croatian Criminal Code, which is series of offences against public safety, and refers to an incident dated 18 October 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And in the fifth column where the details of the victim are normally located, this entry appears to have been partly whited out, and I'm wondering if you have any information or can assist the Chamber in what this entry relates to.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: The person making entries into the register probably made an error and therefore whited it out, which is not proper procedure. One should not white it out by merely cross out an error. However, the entry indicates that the case was referred to the civilian prosecutor's office, i.e., the Zadar Public Prosecutor's Office, under that number. This is merely an opinion I'm offering. In order to verify the actual situation, I would have to look at both the case file and the register.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And more generally, if a military commander or military officer in the Split Military District received information that Split Military District soldiers had committed a crime, or he personally observed them committing a crime in circumstances where he was not aware of their specific identity, would he be able to file a report against unknown perpetrators with the Split Military Prosecutor's Office?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not only could he have filed a report, he must have had -- must have done that, and a report should have contained the elements of the crime and information allowing further inquiries into the -- into the perpetrators and their identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: When you said he -- not only could he have filed a report he must have had -- I would just like to clarify because "must" can have various meanings in English. Do you mean that not only he could have filed a report, he should have had; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'm invoking the Law on Criminal Procedure again, whereby all the public and state agencies have the duty to file a report to the competent body, which includes military bodies; soldiers, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There interpreter notes: The witness also said commanders.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And when you said: "The report should have contained the elements of the crime and information allowing further inquiries into the perpetrators and their identification," would such information, for example, include the unit that the soldiers belonged to, if the commander was aware of the identity of the unit?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could tender this exhibit as well as the KTN register for 1996, which is 65 ter 7373.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter 7372 will become Exhibit P2606; the 65 ter number 7373 becomes P2607.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence, but the Chamber expects a brief report on the issue I just raised.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we'll get that as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is it correctly understood that not all the entries are translated, just the format.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: The format and a number of the abbreviations that are contained --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But not the data contained in the various columns.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least that's what I did not find. For example, the KTN register, it's a three-page document of which the third page is empty. So it's just an explanation of the format, and you have dealt with some of these entries specifically.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And they are -- we did it that way because we simply didn't have time to translate the entire document and also because the entries are largely but not exclusively names and numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Which means that the Chamber, of course, is limited in accessing the data contained in these reports and is focussing mainly at this moment on what kind of registers were kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can request a full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm not insisting on it but I'm just -- usually if an exhibit is tendered and admitted into evidence, we usually have a full translation, which makes every detail of information accessible for the Chamber. I just, at this moment, establish that this is not the case in full with this document -- these documents, I should say. I'm just pointing at the limits in -- Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't want to anticipate further cross-examination, and if I'm mistaken I am sure I will be corrected, but I think there is a chart that's been prepared which will list some of the entries that have been lifted from here, although could I be wrong, and the Prosecution and the Defence are in the process of finalising agreement on which entries are relevant or not relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear. I'm just, at this moment -- we decided to admit something into evidence, and therefore I try to establish what this exactly means with not a full translation of this document available to the Chamber. You may proceed, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, and I thank my colleague as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Mr. Bajic, the Prosecution has examined each of the entries in the KT and KTN registers starting from beginning of August 1995 and going until the end of March -- beginning of August 1995, I should say, and concluding at the end of March 1996, and this analysis indicates that during this period of time no Split Military District units, commanders, or officers reported any crimes relevant to the indictment in this case, which is, roughly speaking, crimes related to looting, destruction, or killing in the area of Sector South in August and September 1995. And I'd just like to ask you if that analysis is in any way inconsistent with your recollection of the reports and cases dealt with by the Split Military Prosecutor at the time?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If we could just get clarification, the question says "did not report," if we could just clarify. The question, I think, is trying to be specific to one institution.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I should clarify that I'm referring to filing criminal reports with the Split Military Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, is the question still clear to you, Mr. Bajic? In the registers on the relevant matters --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me be brief. All the reports received by the Military Prosecutor's Office, either in the form of KT, reports against persons known, or KTN against persons unknown, were registered in our registers. In other words, all the cases received by our office were registered and entered into the registers.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So, in other words, you have no reason to doubt the accuracy of the registers. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No. Let me just make this point. A small number of cases were entered into the KRDO register because it wasn't clear whether they could indeed be qualified as crimes. I also said that a small number of them could have been entered into a strictly confidential register, but the number was so small that it can hardly have an impact on the general picture.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of questions about that. The KRDO register, is that the same thing as the KTR register?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The KTR register is one containing all information, filings and memos sent to the Military Prosecutor's Office which did not belong to the regular registers; primarily the KT containing reports against known persons and KTN against unknown persons. The prosecutors would also take certain steps and inquiries and would seek information in relation to KTR cases in order to find out whether the reports did amount to crimes. Alternatively, if they found that the information was irrelevant, then they would merely make a note on the folder of the case to the effect that there were no further grounds for acting upon that particular report. Let me just state that the KTR register did not, as a rule, contain any reports against individuals known or unknown. All these reports were entered into the two registers you mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the -- so the KRDO register, where you said was used for situations where it was unclear whether it could be qualified as a crime, if you had received a criminal report from a military commander against known or unknown members of the HV for crimes relating to burning, looting, or killing, are there any circumstances where that report could end up in the KRDO register?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No, they would end up in the KT register.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think we get a lot of confusion at this moment. If I invite the parties to look at page 79, line 16, there, it seem what previously was apparently KTN, that is unknown persons, now suddenly appears as KTR, but also linked to unknown persons. Can we try to find -- I do understand, Mr. Bajic, KT register contains all the reports on crimes where perpetrators are known. KT -- I see you're nodding yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. That's the first. KTN is the register in which all reported crimes with unknown perpetrators were registered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: KTR is the register which, I think you called it miscellaneous. That means all type of reporting, filing, et cetera, where it is unclear whether it directly relates to a crime being committed. Is that correctly understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, the last category, and perhaps you would -- that is the KRDO register. Could you try to summarise in one or one line and a half what that register exactly contains.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the same KTR register which was subsequently renamed into KRDO. So it's an identical register, it's the same register, which carried a different designation at different times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Again, then, KRDO also registers miscellaneous reporting, filing, et cetera, where it's unclear whether it can be directly linked to a crime being committed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And one last question, Mr. Bajic, is you referred to: "... a small number of crimes could be entered into a strictly confidential register but the number was so small that it can hardly have an impact." What was the strictly confidential register for?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: It was the register containing a handful or a dozen or so entries based on the documents received by the Military Prosecutor's Office, already bearing the designation "confidential" or "strictly confidential." Under our regulations, where we received documents marked this way, we have to register the case under the -- with the same status until the time when the person sending the document to us asks for the status to be changed, and we had, during a certain period of time, documents that we received and we had to act upon, and they were registered in this way. However, they did not remain in that register for long. It took some time for the case to be investigated into, a month or two, and then it would be transferred to the KT register.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to believe that a criminal report filed by a military commander or officer against an HV member for a crime related to looting, burning, or killing in the aftermath of Operation Storm would be filed within this strictly confidential register?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN BAJIC
utterances.text: No. I can state with a great degree of certainty that the register did not contain such entries. However, there was the possibility for the colleagues working out in the field to make a mistake, because they were not experienced enough. I was involved in some cases where I came upon cases being entered into wrong registers. There were no such entries made that were not supposed to be known, because there were -- simply were not such entries to begin with, and therefore they could not be part of the register.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to move to another topic. I can start now or if you'd rather adjourn for the day ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it would be wiser to -- to finish for the day, and --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Um --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to if Mr. Bajic could be handed a bundle of case files that I will referring to tomorrow so that can he read them in order to expedite matters tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The Defence is familiar with the content of the documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: They're on the cross-examination document list. I'd be happy to provide the numbers to Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. No objections. Now, Mr. Bajic, you get some homework from Ms. Gustafson. Could you please look through it before tomorrow so you will be better able to understand the questions Ms. Gustafson will put to you. May I further urge the Prosecution, once it has made up its mind as far as the next witness is concerned, to inform the Chamber, even informally, and, of course, copying the Defence on its position so that if there's any green light to be switched on, that it can be done as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we adjourn for the day, Mr. Bajic, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00. But I would like to instruct you that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether that is testimony you've given already today, or whether it is about the testimony you're expected to give tomorrow. We adjourn and we resume tomorrow, Tuesday 25th of August, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom III.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 25th day of August, 2009, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.42 p.m.,
